moduleMetadata.title: Industrial & Workplace Cybersecurity
moduleMetadata.description: Cybersecurity Awareness for Industrial, Manufacturing, Engineering & Workplace Personnel
moduleMetadata.whyThisMatters: Industrial organizations increasingly depend on digital technology to operate safely and efficiently. Cybersecurity is not only the responsibility of the IT or cybersecurity department. Every employee can either reduce or increase organizational risk through everyday actions.
moduleMetadata.learningOutcome: After completing this module, employees will be able to recognize common cyber risks in industrial and workplace environments, protect workplace information and devices, avoid unsafe actions, and report problems quickly using the RECOGNIZE → STOP → PRESERVE → REPORT → FOLLOW model.

learningObjectives: Understand why cybersecurity matters in industrial environments.
Understand the difference between ordinary business IT and operational/industrial technology.
Understand how cyber incidents can affect business operations, equipment, people, and safety.

Recognize phishing, social engineering, suspicious USB devices, unauthorized software, suspicious remote-access requests, account compromise, physical-security issues, data leakage, and suspicious system behavior.
Practice secure account usage, safe email behavior, safe USB usage, secure remote working, physical security, data protection, and safe device usage.
Apply the RECOGNIZE → STOP → PRESERVE → REPORT → FOLLOW incident response model.
Know what to include in an incident report and understand that fast reporting — even after a mistake — is always the right choice.

sections.title: Module Purpose
sections.content: Industrial organizations increasingly depend on digital technology to operate safely and efficiently. Employees may interact with:
sections.callout:
Cybersecurity is not only the responsibility of the IT or cybersecurity department. Every employee can either reduce or increase organizational risk through everyday actions.

This module teaches employees how to recognize common cyber risks, protect workplace information and devices, avoid unsafe actions, and report problems quickly.

sections.title: Section 1 — Why Industrial Cybersecurity Matters
sections.content:
An industrial environment is a workplace where technology supports activities such as: Manufacturing; Energy; Construction; Transportation; Telecommunications; Utilities; Warehousing; Engineering; Production; Processing.

Modern organizations may combine physical machinery with digital systems.

For example: Sensor → Network → Computer/System → Employee → Industrial Process

A problem affecting one part of this chain can potentially affect other parts.

subsections.title: Cybersecurity Is More Than Protecting Data
subsections.content: For an ordinary employee, cybersecurity may sound like: 'Protect your password.' In industry, cybersecurity can involve much more. A cyber incident may potentially affect:
bulletPoints: Information — Company files and confidential information.
Equipment — Connected equipment and supporting systems.
People — Employees, contractors, customers, and visitors.
Safety — Some industrial environments have systems where cybersecurity and physical safety can intersect.
subsections.callout: Never treat an industrial cybersecurity problem as 'just a computer problem.'

sections.title: Section 2 — IT and OT: Simple Explanation
sections.content: Understanding the difference between IT and OT helps employees know why different rules apply to different systems.

subsections.title: What Is OT?
subsections.content:
OT = Operational Technology

OT refers broadly to technology used to monitor or control physical processes.

subsections.title: Why Does the Difference Matter?
subsections.content: An employee may be able to restart an office computer without major consequences. The same assumption should not be applied to industrial systems.
subsections.callout: Never restart, modify, disconnect, reconfigure, or update industrial equipment unless you are authorized and trained to do so.

sections.title: Section 3 — The Industrial Cybersecurity Golden Rules
sections.content: These seven rules form the foundation of safe behavior in an industrial workplace.
checklist: Rule 1 — Protect Your Credentials: Never share passwords or authentication codes.
Rule 2 — Verify Unexpected Requests: Don't trust a request simply because it looks professional.
Rule 3 — Don't Connect Unknown Devices: Especially USB/removable media.
Rule 4 — Verify People: Employees, contractors, visitors, and vendors should follow authorization procedures.
Rule 5 — Don't Make Unauthorized Changes: Especially to industrial or production systems.
Rule 6 — Protect Company Information: Share information only with authorized recipients.
Rule 7 — Report Early: A small warning can become a large incident if ignored.

sections.title: Section 4 — Account Security
sections.content:
An employee account may provide access to: Email; Files; Internal applications; Business systems; Communication tools; Industrial-support systems.

Your account should be treated as a security asset.

subsections.title: Password Rules
subsections.content: Use strong, unique passwords and enable MFA wherever available.
dont: Passwords based on easily known personal information

subsections.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
subsections.content:
MFA adds another layer of protection.

Example: Password + Authentication App
or
Password + Security Key
subsections.callout: If you receive an MFA request that you did not initiate: Do not approve it. Report it according to organizational procedures.

sections.title: Section 5 — Phishing in Industry
sections.content:
Attackers may target industrial employees using highly believable messages.

They may impersonate:

subsections.title: Example Industrial Phishing Message
subsections.content:
Subject: URGENT — MACHINE MAINTENANCE DOCUMENT

'Please open the attached document immediately and send the requested information.'

subsections.title: Verify Before Acting — The WHO/WHAT/WHY/WHEN/HOW Framework
subsections.content: Before opening or responding to any unexpected request, ask:
framework: What are they asking me to do?
Does the requested process match normal company procedure?

sections.title: Section 6 — Business Email Compromise
sections.content:
An attacker may compromise or impersonate a legitimate business account.

They could request:
sections.callout:
Example: 'Our bank account has changed. Please use this new account for all future payments.'

Correct Action: Do not rely solely on the email. Verify the request through an approved, independent organizational procedure.

sections.title: Section 7 — Social Engineering
sections.content:
Social engineering means manipulating people into performing an action or revealing information.

Attackers may use:
sections.callout: The Pressure Test: When someone pressures you, ask: 'Would I normally be allowed to do this?' If the answer is unclear: STOP → VERIFY

sections.title: Section 8 — USB & Removable Media
sections.content: USB devices are common in industrial workplaces. They may be used for legitimate purposes, but unknown devices can create security risks.
bulletPoints: Never automatically trust found USB drives
Never automatically trust personal USB drives
Never automatically trust unknown vendor media
Never automatically trust devices given by strangers
Never automatically trust devices that appear 'urgent'
sections.callout:
Golden Rule: If you don't know where a device came from, don't connect it to a company or industrial system.

Follow your organization's approved removable-media process.

sections.title: Section 9 — Unauthorized Software
sections.content:
Employees may encounter software that promises faster performance, free tools, video conversion, remote support, driver updates, file recovery, or security scanning.

But unauthorized software can introduce:
sections.callout: Rule: Use only software approved by your organization.

sections.title: Section 10 — Remote Access
sections.content: Remote access can be necessary for maintenance, technical support, engineering, and administration. But it should be controlled.

sections.title: Section 11 — Vendor & Contractor Security
sections.content:
Industrial organizations frequently work with external parties.

Examples: Equipment manufacturers; Maintenance companies; Contractors; Engineers; Consultants; IT service providers.
sections.callout:
Before providing access: VERIFY → AUTHORIZE → FOLLOW PROCEDURE

Never assume: 'They are a vendor, so they can access everything.'

sections.title: Section 12 — Physical Security
sections.content:
Cybersecurity doesn't stop at the computer screen.

Protect:

subsections.title: Tailgating
subsections.content:
Someone enters a restricted area by following an authorized employee.

Example: 'Hold the door for me; I forgot my card.'

Correct Response: Follow your organization's access-control procedures.

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 13: Clean Desk / Clean Screen
sections.content: Before leaving your workstation:
checklist: Don't leave sensitive information visible to unauthorized people

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 14: Data Protection
sections.content: Employees may handle:

subsections.title: Before Sharing Information — The WHO/WHAT/WHERE/WHY Framework
subsections.content: Ask these questions before sharing any company information:
framework: Does the person need this information?
Am I using an approved communication/storage method?

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 15: Wrong Recipient
sections.content:
An employee intends to email a confidential document to Ali — Finance but accidentally sends it to Ali — External Contractor.

Don't hide the mistake.
sections.callout:
What should happen? Immediately: Stop → Report → Follow Instructions

The organization can then determine the appropriate response.

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 16: Cloud Storage
sections.content:
Employees may use company cloud storage, collaboration platforms, and file-sharing systems.

Risks:
sections.callout: Rule: Use organization-approved storage and sharing methods.

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 17: Mobile Device Security
sections.content: Company phones and tablets may contain sensitive information.

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 18: Lost Device
sections.content:
An employee loses a company laptop containing work files.

Wrong response: 'I'll wait and see if someone returns it.'

Correct response: REPORT IMMEDIATELY
sections.callout: The organization may have procedures to: Disable access; Protect accounts; Remotely manage the device; Assess exposure.

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 19: Remote Work
sections.content: When working outside the workplace, protect:
checklist: Information — Handle data according to company policy
Privacy — Be aware of your surroundings
sections.callout: Be careful around: Public spaces; Shared computers; Public Wi-Fi; Untrusted devices; Shoulder surfing

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 20: Public Wi-Fi
sections.content:
Public Wi-Fi isn't automatically malicious, but it may not provide the same level of trust or control as a managed organizational network.

Follow company policy. Use approved secure connections for work activities where required.

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 21: Suspicious System Behavior
sections.content: Employees should recognize warning signs. Possible signs:

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 22: Don't Become an 'Accidental Investigator'
sections.content: This is particularly important for non-technical employees. If something looks suspicious:
do: STOP — Cease the potentially unsafe action
sections.callout: Let the appropriate technical team investigate.

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 23: Incident Recognition
sections.content: A possible security incident may involve any of the following categories:

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 24: The MilcharSec Incident Model
sections.content: When something goes wrong, follow this five-step model:
framework: Don't continue the potentially unsafe action.

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 25: 'I Made a Mistake'
sections.content:
You clicked a suspicious link. Your first thought: 'I should hide it.'

MilcharSec says: DON'T HIDE IT.

Fast reporting can help the organization respond more effectively.
sections.callout:
Correct behavior: I clicked → I stopped → I reported.

Not: I clicked → I hid it → Problem became bigger.

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 26: Reporting Without Fear
sections.content:
Mistakes happen. Delayed reporting can make them harder to manage.

If you accidentally clicked something suspicious, opened an unexpected attachment, sent information to the wrong person, or connected an unknown device, report it promptly according to your organization's procedures.

sections.title: Session 2 — Section 27: What to Include in a Report
sections.content: Employees don't need to write a technical report. Just answer:
framework: Do you have the email, message, screenshot, filename, or other relevant information?

sections.title: Section 33 — Role-Based Awareness Guide
sections.content: Different roles face different risk profiles. Use the guide for your role to focus your awareness.

rows: USB, Equipment, Remote support, Physical access, Suspicious system behavior
Engineering workstations, Technical information, Remote access, Vendor access, System changes
Executive impersonation, Sensitive information, Payment requests, Incident escalation, Employee reporting
Employee information, Privacy, Phishing, Document security, Identity-related scams
Fake invoices, Payment requests, Bank-detail changes, Business email compromise
Authorization, Device security, Physical access, Data handling, Remote access

sections.title: Section 34 — Who Should I Contact?
sections.content: Use the appropriate reporting channel for your situation:
sections.callout: Your organization should configure the actual contact details. MilcharSec provides the framework; your workplace provides the specifics.

sections.title: Section 36 — Final Industrial Security Checklist
sections.content: Use this checklist to review your current security posture across all key areas.

sections.title: Module Completion — Five Things to Remember
sections.content: After completing Module 10, remember these five principles:
framework: Report problems quickly — even if you made a mistake.
sections.callout:
BEFORE YOU CLICK — THINK
BEFORE YOU CONNECT — VERIFY
BEFORE YOU GIVE ACCESS — AUTHORIZE
BEFORE YOU SHARE — CHECK
WHEN SOMETHING GOES WRONG — STOP → PRESERVE → REPORT

You don't need to be a cybersecurity expert to be part of the defense.

scenarios.title: A Normal Working Day
scenarios.content:
You are starting your shift. Four things happen in quick succession. For each one, decide what the correct response is.

Time: 8:05 AM
Event: You receive an email: 'Urgent maintenance document attached.' The sender is unfamiliar.
Warning sign: Suspicious attachment with urgency from an unexpected sender.
Correct action: Don't open automatically. Verify through a known, official contact before taking any action.

Time: 8:20 AM
Event: Someone you don't recognize hands you a USB drive and says: 'Check this file quickly.'
Warning sign: Unknown removable media from an unverified person.
Correct action: Don't connect it. Follow your organization's removable-media procedure. Verify the person's authorization.

Time: 8:40 AM
Event: A visitor says: 'The manager asked me to access this workstation.' They have no visitor badge.
Warning sign: Authorization issue — claimed verbal approval with no documented authorization.
Correct action: Follow visitor verification procedures. Do not grant access until authorization is properly confirmed.

Time: 9:00 AM
Event: An unexpected security warning appears on your workstation screen.
Warning sign: Possible security incident or malware warning.
Correct action: Stop what you are doing. Preserve the information (screenshot if possible, note the time). Report to IT. Do not attempt to 'fix' it yourself or dismiss it.
scenarios.lesson: Industrial environments present multiple potential threats in a single working day. The response is always the same: RECOGNIZE → STOP → PRESERVE → REPORT → FOLLOW.

quiz.question: What does OT stand for in an industrial context?
options: Online Technology
Operational Technology
Output Terminal
Organizational Tools
quiz.explanation: OT (Operational Technology) refers broadly to technology used to monitor or control physical processes, such as industrial control systems, sensors, and production equipment. It is distinct from IT (Information Technology) used for office and business functions.

quiz.question: You find a USB drive in the company car park. What is the correct action?
options: Plug it in to find out who owns it.
Give it to a colleague to check on their computer.
Do not connect it. Hand it to IT or security according to your organization's procedure.
Take it home.
quiz.correctAnswer: Do not connect it. Hand it to IT or security according to your organization's procedure.
quiz.explanation: Found USB drives are a known social-engineering technique. Plugging in an unknown device — even to identify its owner — can introduce malware. Always follow the organizational procedure for found devices.

quiz.question: You receive an MFA approval notification for an account you are not currently trying to access. What should you do?
options: Approve it — it is probably an IT update.
Ignore it.
Do not approve it. Report the unexpected MFA request according to organizational procedures.
Approve it once and change your password later.
quiz.correctAnswer: Do not approve it. Report the unexpected MFA request according to organizational procedures.
quiz.explanation: An MFA request you did not initiate is a warning sign that someone may be attempting to access your account with stolen credentials. Never approve an MFA request you did not trigger. Report it immediately.

quiz.question: An unknown visitor says: 'I'm from the equipment company.' They have no badge. What should you do?
options: Let them in — they seem legitimate.
Follow your organization's visitor verification and authorization procedures.
Give them access to a workstation so they can start work.
Give them your credentials.
quiz.correctAnswer: Follow your organization's visitor verification and authorization procedures.
quiz.explanation: Access to secure areas must always be verified through proper authorization procedures. Claimed identity is not sufficient — every visitor and contractor must go through the correct verification process.

quiz.question: You accidentally clicked a link in a suspicious email. What is the correct response?
options: Hope nothing happened and continue working.
Delete the email and tell no one.
Stop what you are doing and report it to IT immediately.
Restart your computer and carry on.
quiz.correctAnswer: Stop what you are doing and report it to IT immediately.
quiz.explanation: Fast reporting after accidentally clicking a suspicious link gives the security team the best chance to respond before any potential damage spreads. Never hide mistakes — fast reporting is always the right choice.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the Industrial Cybersecurity Golden Rules?
options: Protect your credentials.
Verify unexpected requests.
Connect unknown devices if they look safe.
Report early.
quiz.correctAnswer: Connect unknown devices if they look safe.
quiz.explanation: The Golden Rules state: never connect unknown devices, especially USB/removable media. How a device 'looks' is not a reliable safety indicator — unknown devices should never be connected to company or industrial systems.

quiz.question: What is the MilcharSec Industrial Incident Model?
options: Report → Fix → Document → Resume
Recognize → Stop → Preserve → Report → Follow
Check → Isolate → Delete → Restart
Notify → Escalate → Investigate → Close
quiz.explanation: The MilcharSec incident model for industrial and workplace environments is: RECOGNIZE (something is wrong), STOP (cease the unsafe action), PRESERVE (keep relevant information), REPORT (tell the appropriate team), and FOLLOW (follow authorized instructions).

quiz.question: A supplier sends an email saying their bank account has changed and requests you update payment details immediately. What should you do?
options: Update the payment details immediately — the email looks official.
Reply to the email to confirm.
Verify the request through an approved, independent organizational procedure — not via the email itself.
Ignore it.
quiz.correctAnswer: Verify the request through an approved, independent organizational procedure — not via the email itself.
quiz.explanation: This is a classic Business Email Compromise (BEC) pattern. Attackers compromise or impersonate supplier accounts and request payment detail changes. Always verify financial requests through an independent, approved channel — never rely solely on the email.

quiz.question: Before leaving your workstation for a meeting, what should you do?
options: Nothing — you will be back soon.
Lock the screen, secure documents, and secure any removable media.
Log out only.
Close all browser tabs.
quiz.correctAnswer: Lock the screen, secure documents, and secure any removable media.
quiz.explanation: The Clean Desk / Clean Screen principle requires locking the screen, securing confidential documents, securing removable media, and protecting access cards before leaving a workstation — regardless of how briefly you will be away.

quiz.question: Which of the following is true about restarting industrial systems?
options: You can restart industrial systems the same way you restart an office computer.
Never restart, modify, disconnect, reconfigure, or update industrial equipment unless you are authorized and trained to do so.
Restarting industrial systems is always safe.
It is fine to restart industrial systems if it seems like the right thing to do.
quiz.correctAnswer: Never restart, modify, disconnect, reconfigure, or update industrial equipment unless you are authorized and trained to do so.
quiz.explanation: Unlike an office computer restart, unauthorized changes to industrial systems can have consequences for production, equipment, and in some environments, safety. Only authorized, trained personnel should make changes to industrial systems.

keyTakeaways: Cybersecurity is everyone's responsibility — not just IT. Every employee can reduce or increase organizational risk.
IT (business systems) and OT (operational/industrial systems) require different levels of caution. Never make unauthorized changes to industrial equipment.
The Industrial Cybersecurity Golden Rules: Protect credentials, Verify requests, Refuse unknown USB devices, Verify people, Avoid unauthorized changes, Protect information, Report early.
Phishing in industrial environments may impersonate managers, suppliers, or maintenance companies — always apply the WHO/WHAT/WHY/WHEN/HOW verification framework.
Found or unknown USB devices must never be connected to company or industrial systems.
The incident response model is: RECOGNIZE → STOP → PRESERVE → REPORT → FOLLOW.
Fast reporting — even after making a mistake — is always better than hiding it. Delayed reporting makes incidents harder to manage.
Clean Desk / Clean Screen: lock your workstation, secure documents, and secure removable media whenever you leave your desk.
Never authorize access to visitors, contractors, or vendors without proper verification — regardless of claimed authority.
reflectApply: Think about your typical working day. How many of the situations described in this module — unexpected emails, USB devices, visitors, system warnings — have you encountered? Which of the Golden Rules would help you respond better?

Identify the correct incident-reporting contact in your organization for each category: IT problem, cybersecurity problem, industrial system problem, and physical security issue. Write them down and keep them accessible.
Review your current account security: is MFA enabled on your work accounts? Is your workstation password unique? Do you lock your screen when you leave your desk?
